proposed_edges.relationship: A settler-colonial analytic worked out in conversation with Native American and Indigenous Studies: US Indian policy (removal, allotment, blood quantum, termination) read as successive modalities of elimination (2006, 2011); 'a key scholar in conceiving of a settler-colonial analytic in relation to Indigenous thinking' (Goeman, 2016)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Goeman 2016 (read in full): "a key scholar in conceiving of a settler-colonial analytic in relation to Indigenous thinking and scholarship that exists far longer than settler nations"; "He critically engaged our field in a respectful and nuanced manner". Kauanui 2016 (read in full), note 7: "his long time, direct intellectual engagement with scholars in Native American and Indigenous Studies", and para. 2: he insisted "that Native scholars did" create the field. Wolfe 2006 (read in full), sections on discovery and preemption, the Cherokee removal, allotment, blood quantum ("statistical extermination", quoting Jaimes) and termination; "After the Frontier" (2011) is unread. A contribution to the conversation, not an origin: the entry's Indigenous methods are not derived from him, and the dissent of Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel (2014) is recorded on the entry. Replaces the former comparison row. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Race as the outcome of 'differentiation, which is an intensely conflictual process' (2001): 'a race cannot be taken as given. It is made in the targeting'; Black people 'racialized as slaves', Indians eliminated 'as Indians' (2006); a comparative typology of colonial race regimes in Traces of History (2016)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full), opening section: "different racial regimes encode and reproduce the unequal relationships into which Europeans coerced the populations concerned"; "Black people's enslavement produced an inclusive taxonomy … For Indians, in stark contrast, non-Indian ancestry compromised their indigeneity"; "a race cannot be taken as given. It is made in the targeting"; and note 62 quoting his own 2001 essay, p. 894: "Difference … is not simply given. It is the outcome of differentiation, which is an intensely conflictual process." The 2001 essay is otherwise unread (Crossref: AHR 106:3, June 2001). Traces of History (2016) known through the British Library contents note (chapters on Australia, the United States, central Europe, Brazil, Palestine) and Veracini's obituary (read): it "utilises his analysis of racism under settler colonialism in order to explain racism everywhere else" and provides "a compelling typology of racial formations". Strengthens the entry-level comparison edge_885, which stays. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Settler colonialism set beside genocide studies: the Holocaust as 'the non-paradigmatic paradigm' against which 'qualified genocides' are devalued; 'structural genocide' proposed to retain settler colonialism's specificity without 'hierarchy among victims'; a chapter in Moses's Empire, Colony, Genocide (2006–08)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full): "Settler colonialism is inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal"; "The best known of all genocides was internal to Europe"; Lemkin's definition (note 6); Hull, Pohl, Zimmerer and "the modernity of colonialism"; "the Holocaust, the non-paradigmatic paradigm that, being the indispensable example, can never merely exemplify"; "the term 'structural genocide' avoids the questions of degree—and, therefore, of hierarchy among victims" (p. 403 per Kauanui). The 2008 chapter in Moses ed. is unread (Berghahn contents; Docker's "Are Settler-Colonies Inherently Genocidal?" in the same volume). The holocaust entry is historiographical; this compares frames and does not claim he wrote Holocaust history. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Settler against franchise colonialism: settler colonies 'were not primarily established to extract surplus value from indigenous labour' but 'premised on displacing indigenes from (or replacing them on) the land' (1999), 'a specific social formation' whose specificity is to be retained (2006)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Wolfe 1999, pp. 1–2 (existing reading, cpl129_wolfe_1999_intro: the introduction distinguishes settler from franchise colonies) and p. 3 as quoted by Englert 2020 (read): "In contrast to the kind of colonial formation that Cabral or Fanon confronted settler colonies were not primarily established to extract surplus value from indigenous labour. Rather, they are premised on displacing indigenes from (or replacing them on) the land". Wolfe 2006 (read in full): "settler colonialism is a specific social formation and it is desirable to retain that specificity". Englert finds the Fanon/Algeria example contradictory (Algeria depended on Indigenous labour). A comparison, not a critique: Hoxie 2008 (existing abstract) places the frame inside postcolonial critique, while Veracini's claim that postcolonial studies missed the settler situation is drawn at entry level (edge_882 revised). (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Treaties, preemption, removal and allotment read as 'the logic of elimination' rather than as relations and encounter: 'the murderous activities of the frontier rabble constitute [the colonial state's] principal means of expansion' (2006); set against the fur-trade historiography's 'middle ground', which Veracini records as a rival recovery (2013)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full), second section (the doctrine of discovery, preemption, the Cherokee removal: "The American right to buy always superseded the Indian right not to sell" (Rosenthal, quoted); "Rather than something separate from or running counter to the colonial state, the murderous activities of the frontier rabble constitute its principal means of expansion") and sixth section (allotment, blood quantum, termination). Veracini 2013, concluding section (author manuscript, read): "the recovery of a long lasting 'middle ground' between indigenous and settler polities in the past, sustained the possibility of renewed relationships"; "both the Canadian and US historiographies were late in adopting settler colonialism as a category of analysis". edge_869 already compares the two fields; this names the person's own reading. Canadian material is not his. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

proposed_edges.relationship: Wolfe took from Harris the sentence that 'the principal momentum of settler colonialism comes into focus' when capital's interest in uncluttered access to land is combined with settlers' interest in land as livelihood (2004, quoted 2006): a use as evidence, moderate
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full), third section and note 36, quoting Harris, "How Did Colonialism Dispossess?" (2004), p. 179: "Combine capital's interest in uncluttered access to land and settlers' interest in land as livelihood, and the principal momentum of settler colonialism comes into focus." Englert 2020 (read) also uses Harris 2004, p. 172, against Wolfe. The direction matters for edge_1014, which found no derivation of Harris from Wolfe: the citation runs the other way. A single quotation; influence in the sense of a use as evidence, as for locB_rel_26 in revision 1.152. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

screq_wolfe_2006.note: Read in full on 2026-10-23 in the Internet Archive capture of 28 June 2025 of the journal's own free-to-read full-text page (http://web.archive.org/web/20250628134148/https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14623520601056240; the live page returned 403; OpenAlex marks the article open on the publisher's site). Notes 1–80 present; the capture carries no page breaks: every page number given for this article in this packet is borrowed from a named reader's citation, not seen in the capture: Kauanui 2016, notes 3–6 (pp. 387, 388, 390, 403) and Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel 2014 (p. 388); Englert 2020 cites p. 393 for the 'inclusive, land-centred project' sentence. Wolfe's own words: "Settler colonialism is inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal" (p. 387); "a race cannot be taken as given. It is made in the targeting"; "Territoriality is settler colonialism's specific, irreducible element"; "settler colonizers come to stay: invasion is a structure not an event" (p. 388; note 7 refers to the 1999 book, p. 2, and the 1994 essay, p. 96); "Settler colonialism destroys to replace"; "elimination refers to more than the summary liquidation of Indigenous people, though it includes that" (p. 390); Cole Harris 2004, p. 179, quoted (note 36); "assimilation's Faustian bargain"; "Richard Pratt and Phillip Sheridan were both practitioners of genocide. The question of degree is not the definitional issue"; "settler colonialism is relatively impervious to regime change"; "the Holocaust, the non-paradigmatic paradigm"; "structural genocide" (p. 403); "settler colonialism is an indicator". The earlier note's attestation through Kauanui's abstract is superseded. See data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md §1.

screq_wolfe_2016.note: Imprint year confirmed as 2016 by the British Library record (p4b_wolfe_traces_bl_2016; electronic edition seen 27 January 2016) and by Goeman 2016, note 6. Contents known from the BL note; unread.

screq_kauanui_2016.note: Full text read on 2026-10-23 (open access, CC BY 4.0; unpaginated web text; notes 1–17). Wolfe "insisted on making it clear time and again that he did not create the field of settler colonial studies—that Native scholars did"; the phrase "structure not an event" "often seems to stand-in for a serious engagement of his theory"; "Settler Colonial Studies does not, should not, and cannot replace Indigenous Studies"; indigeneity "distinct from race, ethnicity, and nationality"; note 7 (Sayegh 1965, Rodinson 1973, Sayigh 1979, Sakai 1983, Trask, Fujikane and Okamura 2008, Veracini 2006 before Wolfe); note 8 (Wolfe's The Settler Complex answers the binary charge); Warrior's 2015 ASA count; NAISA founded 2008 (note 10); acknowledgements dated to "the immediate wake of Patrick Wolfe's death". She calls him "the late English scholar"; Wikidata records an Australian historian born in Yorkshire.

screq_harris_2004.note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full) quotes p. 179 approvingly (note 36): "Combine capital's interest in uncluttered access to land and settlers' interest in land as livelihood, and the principal momentum of settler colonialism comes into focus"; Englert 2020 cites p. 172 for Indigenous incorporation into the workforce. The direction of use runs Harris → Wolfe.

people_update.identity_note: Australian historian (1949–2016) of settler colonialism, race and the history of anthropology; born in Yorkshire, educated at the LSE and the University of Melbourne (Wikidata Q109284663); research and teaching positions at Victoria University, the University of Melbourne and La Trobe University (Victoria University collection page).
